question: What has to change in a project's delivery to adopt a robotic process?

answer.answer:
Adopting a robotic process is mostly an organisational change, not a purchase. Of the cited requirements of robotic assembly (PR4), only one, the robotic arm (RE2), is a machine: the others are the delivery/business model/work culture itself (RI12), highly standardised work (AT7), prefabrication/off-site (PR2), path-planning (PR12) and a mobile factory (CO12). The delivery link is asserted far more than it is exhibited: robotic assembly's dependence on delivery/business model/work culture is carried by 2 of the 50 coded cases and the mobile factory precondition by none, while 16 cases draw on delivery/business model/work culture in its own right and 44 on required workforce training (RI6). In practice the levers with the most support are early contractor involvement (CO11), vertical integration (CO10) feeding an integrated design-DFAB process (AT12), a DFAB design coordinator (AC4) and training, with higher management complexity (RI4) as the cost.

**The direct delivery dependency, and how thin it is**

PR4 "Robotic assembly" dependsOn RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture", on the ground that robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context; the edge is backed by peer-reviewed evidence and carried by 2 of the 50 coded cases. [1] RI12 is the requirement here and sits upstream of the robotic process. RI12 carries 2 inbound and 0 outbound edges in total, and 16 of the 50 coded cases draw on it. [1] The second of those two inbound edges is the more heavily exhibited one: AT8 "Industrialised" dependsOn RI12, because adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models, carried by 13 of the 50 cases [1]. So the business-model change is evidenced much more strongly as a condition of operating at industrialised scale (AT8 is drawn on by 23 of the 50 cases) [1] than as a condition tied to robotic assembly specifically.

**What else robotic assembly requires, and the asymmetry between those requirements**

Taking PR4 as the single anchor, its cited requirements and their carried counts are: the robotic arm (RE2), carried by 12 of the 50 [1]; highly standardised work (AT7), carried by 10, on the evidence that Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components [1]; prefabrication/off-site (PR2) as a precondition, carried by 4, since automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [1]; path-planning (PR12), carried by 2 [1]; delivery/business model/work culture (RI12), carried by 2; and the mobile factory condition (CO12), carried by 0 of the 50, cited for all-weather cover allowing welding and assembly to proceed in rain [1]. CO12 is a direct cited precondition of PR4, not an indirect one, and no case in the record carries it. The enablers themselves are unevenly drawn on: PR12 by 26 of the 50 [1], AT7 by 25 [1], RE2 by 22 [1], PR2 by 20 [1], RI12 by 16, and CO12 by 1 [1], against 13 that draw on PR4 itself [1].

**The delivery changes with the strongest support**

Early contractor involvement is the clearest procurement change: CO11 "Early contractor involvement" enablesCapability PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", carried by 13 of the 50, on the argument that integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in the early design phase and that a delivery method involving participants in early design should be selected [1]. CO11 also enables PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process", carried by 11 [1], and AT12 "Integrated design-DFAB process", carried by 10 [1]. 14 of the 50 cases draw on CO11. [1]

Contractual and organisational coupling runs alongside it: AT12 hasPrecondition CO10 "Vertical integration", carried by 14, because technically interdependent systems require tighter organisational coupling such as a single firm [1], with the reciprocal edge CO10 enablesCapability AT12 also carried by 14 [1]. A role change appears too: AC4 "DFAB design coordinator" enablesCapability AT12, carried by 7, via interdisciplinary team integration [1], though only 8 of the 50 cases draw on AC4 [1].

**Workforce, safety and the management overhead**

AR9 "Automated production workflow" dependsOn RI6 "Require workforce training", carried by 38 of the 50, because the sophistication of digital technologies prohibits adoption by less technologically familiar workers [1], and CO6 "Human-robot interaction" dependsOn RI6, carried by 27, since human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce [1]. 44 of the 50 cases draw on RI6 [1], making training the single best-supported change here. Where people work beside the machine, CO6 also dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", carried by 2, on compliance with robot safety standards [1], and CO6 mitigates RI20 "Work safety concern", carried by 4, through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation [1]; RI20 carries three cited edges in total and only this one is in front of me. The cost side is visible but unconnected: 15 of the 50 cases draw on RI4 "Increase management complexity", which carries no cited dependency edge at all [1], so the literature has not linked it, and its support rests on that count and on correlation.

**The deployed record**

The census records here are deployed robotic processes at high readiness but the context does not link any of them to these enablers, so none can be said to exhibit RI12. census_RXH4-1 is a deployed robotic construction process adopted to address cost and labor, performing assembly and concrete work on the structural core and the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, at technology readiness level 9 [2], with Firm_166 as manufacturer and concrete as its material [3]. census_RXH7-2 was adopted to address quality, safety, labor and market, and performs assembly and tiling on the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, at technology readiness level 9 [4]; it is the census record of RP29, manufactured by Firm_125, using ceramic and steel [3]. That both were adopted against labour and market drivers rather than purely technical ones is consistent with the delivery-model argument, but it is not the same as the record carrying that edge.

One scope note: retrieval widened "robotic process" beyond robotic assembly, and of the others only the robotic arm (RE2) and RE10 "Gantry-type robotic system", drawn on by 5 of the 50 cases and carrying no dependency edges [1], have counts in front of me; the retrieved material does not cover delivery-side edges for the remaining robotic resources, so this answer does not establish that none exist.
